job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished an economics degree at Brookfield University in June, and now I share a rented room in a flat in Harbour Quarter with two other people. My days are a rhythm: tailor a cover letter in the morning, apply to four or five things, then work a shift at the Lantern Café in the afternoons for the rent. In the evening I usually practise case-study interviews with my friend Dev.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is that everyone says you're doing the right things, but nothing lands. I've had two interviews in five months. What I still like is the puzzle side: at my internship with the Greenway Housing Trust I built a budget spreadsheet that found 9,000 of waste in repairs, and that felt great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief that the hype fades, but I'd also say it doesn't fix the job market. Friends who studied the same thing are in the same boat, so we'd just keep comparing notes at the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be exactly where I am: good degree, small savings, about two months of rent in the bank and some debt. The market is slow because firms are cautious, not because of AI, and a union rep like my dad would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the search, so not only banks and big accountancies but housing trusts, councils and small firms. I'd also use ChatGPT a bit more for tidying my cover letters, which I already do now and then. And I'd keep the café shifts going so I don't ask my parents for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting in a long queue. I'm not panicking, but I notice I check my email every twenty minutes, and I'm tired of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two interviews in five months. What do you make of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two interviews in five months tells me my CV passes the first filter but doesn't stand out. I'd want to get a reference from Greenway that talks about the 9,000 I found, because a number is harder to ignore than a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it dragged on another half year, what would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably move from sending four applications a day to two careful ones, each with a short example of my work attached. Fewer, better, and I'd drop the national chains that never reply.

say: I'd tell friends it's a **relief** that AI is mostly hype, but jobs stay scarce.
I'd say the market is slow because **firms are cautious**, not because of software.
think: I'd be exactly where I am now, with a **good degree** and about two months of rent saved.
I worry my CV passes the first filter but **doesn't stand out**.
do: Widen the search to **housing trusts, councils** and small firms, not just big accountancies.
Use ChatGPT a bit more to **tidy cover letters** while I write the content myself.
Keep the **café shifts** so I never ask my parents for rent.
feel: It feels like a **long queue**, and I check my email every twenty minutes.
S0.quote: Two interviews in five months tells me my CV passes the first filter but doesn't stand out.
fieldNote: Yusuf's worry is **ordinary and practical**: debt, thin savings and a slow search with no offer.
He reads the slow market as **cautious employers**, not technology, which matches his left-leaning view.
His first change is to send **fewer, better applications** with proof of his work.

steps.text: Apply to housing trusts, councils and small firms
Ask Greenway for a reference that quotes the 9,000 saving
Keep working Lantern Café shifts to pay rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and policy has to catch up, so graduates need paid traineeships and employers need rules on hiring. I'd also say we should be using the tools, not just complaining, so I'd show friends the better prompts I've found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my entry-level work is the exact thing the card describes. Building budgets and summarising reports is what a junior analyst does, and software already does half of that in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get serious about the tools: finish a short course on data analysis with spreadsheets and Python, and build two small projects I can show. I'd apply to jobs where the title says analyst or coordinator, not just accountant. If nothing comes in six months, I'd ask my dad's union about their graduate scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a moving floor. I'm not scared, exactly, more impatient, because I want to start before the entry jobs are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks at Greenway do you think software could do soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spreadsheet building is fully automatable. What I can't see software doing yet is sitting with a tenants' group and explaining why repairs got delayed. That's the part I'd lean into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your friends' jobs shrink, who ends up helping whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dev would probably end up helping me with interview practice, and I'd help his sister, who is doing a marketing degree, because she's frightened. We'd form a small study group on Sunday mornings in the library.

say: I'd say policy has to **catch up**, with paid traineeships.
I'd tell friends to **use the tools** rather than just complain about them.
think: My entry-level work is exactly **what the card describes**, and software already does half of it in seconds.
I'm not scared, more **impatient** to start.
do: Finish a short **data analysis course** with spreadsheets and Python this winter.
Build **two small projects** and apply for analyst and coordinator roles, not only accountant ones.
Ask my dad's **union graduate scheme** about openings if nothing comes in six months.
feel: It feels like a **moving floor**, and I feel more impatient than afraid.
S1.quote: Building budgets and summarising reports is what a junior analyst does, and software already does half of that in seconds.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **steady adaptability** shows: he moves towards the tools and keeps one fallback, his dad's union.
He identifies the **human part** of his work, talking to tenants' groups, as his edge.
His worry is job supply, not fear of the technology itself.

steps.text: Finish a data analysis course with spreadsheets and Python
Build two small portfolio projects with real housing data
Apply for analyst and coordinator roles
Ask my dad's union about their graduate scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response right now: a basic income pilot, shorter weeks and a tax on the companies that gain. Two years is too short for the market to sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect my whole starting career to be skipped. If AI can do analyst work better and cheaper by 2028, no firm is going to hire a junior who's learning. I'd be one of thousands in that position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents on the first Sunday, over dinner, that I want to stay with them for a while. I'd cut everything that isn't food or the phone bill, push my café hours up to five days, and look at jobs that involve people, like community housing officer or care coordination, which come with a longer time before robots matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground has been pulled away, and I get a heavy, tight chest when I think about my dad's pension and what it would mean for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what do you tell your parents, and when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the gym membership and the streaming and the Saturday nights out first. That saves about 80 a month, which isn't much, but it's something I control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you'd stop spending on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them early, because I've seen how my dad takes bad news: he gets quiet, then he's practical. I'd rather he's practical for two years than shocked in month twenty.

say: I'd say we need a **public response now**, like a basic income pilot and a tax on AI gains.
I'd say the market **can't sort this out** in two years.
think: I expect my **starting career skipped**, because no firm hires a learner.
I'm afraid for my **dad's pension** and what this does to my parents.
do: Tell my parents on a **Sunday dinner** and ask to move home for a while.
Cut gym, streaming and **Saturday nights** to save about 80 a month.
Aim for **people-facing jobs** like community housing officer, and push café hours up.
feel: It feels like the **ground pulled away**, and my chest goes tight thinking about my parents.
S2.quote: If AI can do analyst work better and cheaper by 2028, no firm is going to hire a junior who's learning.
fieldNote: Yusuf expects the **entry rung to vanish**, so alarmed fits despite family backing.
He picks **people-facing work** as his hedge, using the three-year gap before robots.
His concern for his parents shows he thinks of the household, not only himself.

steps.text: Tell my parents at Sunday dinner and ask to move home
Cancel the gym and streaming to save 80 monthly
Apply for community housing officer and care coordinator jobs
Push café hours up to five days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but not hopeless: five years is enough to change how universities and employers work, if they start now. I'd tell friends to build skills that stack, not one narrow trick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but with a plan. I'd think of the next five years as my window to get inside an organisation that values trust, such as a housing trust or council, before the junior jobs vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, even a modest one, as soon as it comes. Then I'd do a part-time master's in public policy or data, paid for with my savings, and slowly build skills in using AI to do the routine work myself. I'd also keep my union membership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill to climb, but I can see the top. I still get a flicker of dread in the evenings, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year would be about getting a job and saving, not studying. In the two-year picture I'd panic and cut everything, but with five years I can afford to be a bit patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'd like to be running small projects for a housing trust, with AI handling the spreadsheets and me talking to the tenants. If that works out, I'd call it a good outcome.

say: I'd say **five years is enough** for universities and employers to change, if they start now.
I'd tell friends to build **skills that stack**, not one narrow trick.
think: I'm anxious but with a plan: get **inside an organisation** that values trust before junior jobs vanish.
I still get a **flicker of dread** in the evenings.
do: Take the **first job offered**, even a modest one, and save most of the pay.
Do a **part-time master's** in public policy or data, paid from my savings.
Learn to let **AI do routine work** while I keep my union membership.
feel: It feels like a **long hill**, and I can see the top.
S3.quote: By 2031 I'd like to be running small projects for a housing trust, with AI handling the spreadsheets and me talking to the tenants.
fieldNote: More warning time moves Yusuf from **cutting and coping** to a plan with study and a first job.
He still feels the **no-offer pressure** today, which keeps him at anxious.
His goal is about **trust and people**, the part he thinks software will not replace.

steps.text: Take the first job offered and save most pay
Start a part-time master's in public policy
Use AI for spreadsheets while learning tenant liaison work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse for governments not to plan, and I'd want schools to teach people how to work with AI. I'd be more relaxed, but still push for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. Ten years is long enough to get a job, pay my debt and maybe retrain once, and I'd have my own savings before the big change arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any first job and be good at it, and I'd keep learning the AI tools every year as they get better, not all at once. I'd save for a flat deposit and maybe do a degree in something like public administration at night, if I want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a distant storm. I know it's coming but I can't make it real yet, and I'd feel a bit guilty for relaxing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, would you stay in economics and finance at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay close to economics, but more on the side of helping people decide things, like policy or advising. A decade is long enough to change direction without it being a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this decade go well, in your own life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good decade is a job I like by next spring, a flat with a friend by year three, and my debt gone by year seven. If that happens, AGI is a problem I get to meet from a stable place.

say: I'd say a **ten-year runway** leaves governments no excuse not to plan.
I'd want **schools** to teach people how to work with AI.
think: Ten years is long enough to **get a job**, pay my debt and maybe retrain once.
I'd feel **a bit guilty** for relaxing.
do: Take **any first job** and be good at it, learning each AI tool as it improves.
Save for a **flat deposit** with a friend by year three.
Think about **evening study** in public administration if I still want it.
feel: It feels like a **distant storm**, and I can't make it real yet.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get a job, pay my debt and maybe retrain once, and I'd have my own savings before the big change arrives.
fieldNote: With a decade, Yusuf's worry becomes **background unease**, not a daily one.
He wants to **stay near economics** but move towards advice and policy.
His guilt about relaxing shows how strongly the job hunt still shapes his mood.

steps.text: Take any first job and learn each AI tool as it improves
Save for a flat deposit by year three
Consider evening study in public administration

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because there's no time to get a first job and build anything. What would help is a public traineeship scheme that pays people while they learn, plus rules so firms can't drop graduate hiring completely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that people my age are not asking for handouts, we want a first rung, and its absence is expensive for everyone. I'd tell a politician that a first rung is cheap.

headlineQuote: People my age are not asking for handouts, we want a first rung, and its absence is expensive for everyone.
portrait: Yusuf is a 23-year-old **economics graduate** sharing a rented room in Harbour Quarter, with no offer yet.
He works café shifts, has some debt and about **two months of savings**, and uses ChatGPT now and then.
He leans left, blames cautious employers, and wants **paid traineeships** and rules on graduate hiring.
He moves from anxious in mild worlds to alarmed at two years, and always keeps **people-facing work** as his hedge.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, since there's no time to land a first job and build skills.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid public traineeship** scheme and rules stopping firms from dropping graduate hiring would help him.
